What strange corner of the universe is this expedition headed for? It's a cozy little planet called `text(Earth)` and a spot `text(miles)` under the surface of the Pacific Ocean called the Mariana Trench.
A HOLE IN THE OCEAN FLOOR

In `1872`, the HMS Challenger expedition set out to map the ocean floor. The explorers spent `text(four years)` crisscrossing the globe, sailing `text(70,000 miles)` (`text(112,654 kilometers)`) - `text(one-third)` of the distance to the moon. It was backbreaking, boring work. Sail about `text(200 miles)` (`text(322 kilometers)`), drop a weighted rope into the water. Measure how much rope it took to hit the bottom. Sail another `text(200 miles)` and do it again. And again. This expedition was a total snooze fest, until a `text(day)` in `1875` about `text(200 miles)` off the coast of Guam. That morning, when the rope was dropped, the ocean swallowed up `text(miles)` of it - `text(five miles)` to be exact. The Challenger's crew had discovered a “hole” in the ocean floor.

It wasn't until the `text(1950s)` that we knew just how big Challenger's discovery was. Using sonar (an instrument that sends out sound waves and measures how long it takes them to come back), scientists discovered that the hole is actually a trench. It is `text(twice)` as long as the state of California and `text(43 miles)` (`text(69 kilometers)`) wide. Parts of the trench are only `text(five miles)` deep, but at its southern end, the trench drops to almost `text(seven miles)`. That means if you planted Mount Everest on the bottom and stacked `text(three)` Empire State buildings on top, you still wouldn't reach the surface of the ocean.

In `1960`, `text(two)` brave explorers, Jacques Piccard and Lt. Don Walsh, became the `text(first)` human beings to see the trench with their own eyes. It took `text(years)` to design and test a submersible ship strong enough to survive the immense water pressure in the trench. Called the Trieste, their ship weighed `text(150 tons)`, including fuel, and was almost `text(60 feet)` (`text(18 meters)`) long. But for all its size, the `text(two)` hydronauts¹ would spend their journey in a round capsule only `text(six feet)` in diameter. That's about the same amount of room `text(per person)` that you'd find inside a refrigerator.

Crammed into that small space, at temperatures not much warmer than those in a fridge, it took the `text(two)` explorers `text(four hours)` and `text(forty-eight minutes)` to descend the `text(6.77 miles)` (`text(11 kilometers)`) into Challenger Deep-the deepest spot in the Mariana Trench. Unfortunately, during the `text(20 minutes)` they spent at the ocean bottom, the `text(two)` hydronauts couldn't see much. The engines on the Trieste stirred up silt from the ocean floor and turned the water into what they described as swirling milk. But even though the Trieste didn't have the ability to take pictures outside the cabin, Piccard and Walsh got a chance to take the `text(first)` deep-sea selfie.

In `2012`, film director and explorer James Cameron led the `text(second)` human expedition (and the `text(first)` solo dive) into the Challenger Deep. It took him `text(half)` the time to reach the bottom, `text(two-and-a-half hours)`, and he did it in a ship that weighed less than `text(one-tenth)` what the Trieste did. Surrounded by water pressure `text(1,000)` times greater than at the ocean surface, he spent `text(three hours)` filming and taking scientific samples.

With `text(six)` high-definition cameras, Cameron and his team filmed some of the deepest-dwelling creatures in existence, including a giant amoeba-like xenophyophore² `text(four inches)` (`text(10 centimeters)`) wide and a unique sea cucumber.
And since the Trieste explorers had already taken the `text(first)` undersea selfie, Cameron's Twitter feed captured the moment he touched the ocean floor: “Hitting bottom never felt so good.”
